ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: A certain student made a simple electric motor by himself, as shown in the figure. In it, the rectangular coil is wound from one enameled wire; the two ends of the enameled wire are respectively led out from the middle positions of one pair of opposite sides of the coil, and serve as the rotating shafts of the coil. Now the coil is set between two metal supports; at this time the plane of the coil is in a vertical plane, and a permanent magnet is placed below the coil. In order to make the coil rotate continuously after the battery is connected to the two metal supports, this student should ( )
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: scrape off the insulating paint on the lower sides of both the left and right rotating shafts

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: A certain student made a simple electric motor by himself, as shown in the figure. In it, the rectangular coil is wound from one enameled wire; the two ends of the enameled wire are respectively led out from the middle positions of one pair of opposite sides of the coil, and serve as the rotating shafts of the coil. Now the coil is set between two metal supports; at this time the plane of the coil is in a vertical plane, and a permanent magnet is placed below the coil. In order to make the coil rotate continuously after the battery is connected to the two metal supports, how should this student scrape off the insulating paint on the left and right rotating shafts?
ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: scrape off the insulating paint on the lower sides of both the left and right rotating shafts
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the rectangular coil is placed vertically, and on the left and right sides there is respectively a section of horizontal rotating shaft formed by the end of the enameled wire, labeled “left rotating shaft” and “right rotating shaft”; the left and right rotating shafts are set on two metal supports, and the supports hold up the rotating shafts from below; a permanent magnet is placed below the coil, and at the lower left there is also a battery connected to the supports. Then reason: The surface of the enameled wire has insulating paint; only when the part where the insulating paint has been scraped off contacts the metal support is the circuit closed. To make the coil rotate continuously, one cannot let the coil be supplied in every half-turn with current in the opposite direction, otherwise the torque will reverse and hinder the rotation; the two rotating shafts should be made to conduct simultaneously in the same half-turn, and to disconnect simultaneously in the other half-turn, using inertia to pass through the power-off half-turn, forming a simple commutation effect. Since in the figure the metal supports contact the lower sides of the rotating shafts, the insulating paint on the lower sides of both the left and right rotating shafts should be scraped off.
